# Naming & Ubiquitous Language

*LLM first draft · human-edited once · frozen*

## The cheapest change with the highest leverage

Renaming is the cheapest change you can make to a codebase: no behavior
moves, and with the Test Suite at the Target Interface, nothing breaks.
It is also the highest-leverage change, because a name is read hundreds
of times for every one time it is written — by you, by the next reader,
and by every AI you collaborate with. A model prompted in the domain's
own terms writes code you do not have to translate back; a model prompted
over `Manager`s and `ProcessData`s guesses. This Module is about
choosing names from one shared vocabulary — a **Ubiquitous Language** —
and holding every class, method, and variable to it.

## One concept, one name — everywhere

A Ubiquitous Language is a single agreed list of terms for the concepts
in your domain, used everywhere: in conversation, in documents, in commit
messages, and in code. One concept gets exactly one name, and one name
means exactly one concept. When the domain says **loan**, the code says
`Loan` — not `Record` in one file, `Entry` in another, and
`LoanDto` in a third. When a concept has no name yet, you name it
first, then code it.

The payoff is mechanical, not aesthetic:

- Search for a domain term and you find every place the code touches
  that concept — grep becomes a design tool.
- A sentence spoken by a domain expert translates into code almost word
  for word, and back again.
- A new reader predicts what a method does from its signature alone,
  before opening the body.

## Four checks that need no taste

A good name states what the reader would otherwise discover by reading
the implementation. A bad name forces that reading — or lies, so the
reader trusts it and is wrong. You do not need taste to tell them apart:

1. **The prediction check.** Read only the name and signature and write
   down what you expect the member to do. Then read the body. Anything
   the body did that your prediction missed — or promised that the body
   skipped — is a naming defect, whichever direction it runs.
2. **The synonym count.** Pick one domain concept and search for every
   word the code uses for it. A count above one means every caller
   carries a translation table the code could have made unnecessary.
3. **The vague-word grep.** Search for `Manager`, `Helper`, `Util`,
   `Handler`, `Process`, `Data`, `Info`, `temp`, `flag`,
   `item`. Each hit names *that a thing exists*, not what it is or
   does. Ask of each: which noun or verb in this member's one-sentence
   job description is missing from its name?
4. **The scope-honesty check.** Count the side effects the name does not
   mention — a `Get` that creates, a `Validate` that saves. Any
   count above zero is a lie the codebase tells hundreds of times.

## A name that will not come is a design probe

Naming is not decoration on top of design — it is the cheapest design
review you can run. When a class cannot be named without *and*, *or*, or
a vague word, it usually holds more than one responsibility; the missing
name is telling you where to split. State each class's responsibility in
one sentence starting with its name: a sentence that needs "and" was two
classes. And when two modules use different words for the same concept,
the boundary between them forces every caller to translate — the
vocabulary clash marks the seam that needs one owner.

## How this runs in your Exercises

- In the refactor-type Exercise the behavior is already correct and the
  Test Suite starts green — the planted Smell is entirely in the names.
  The Target Interface's names are the Ubiquitous Language; rename
  everything behind it into that language, suite green after each step.
- In the construct-type Exercise the temptation is to let implementation
  vocabulary write the code: `dict`, `entry`, `flag`, a helper
  named `Manager`. The folder's glossary is the domain's language —
  every name you introduce draws from it.
- Either way, finish with the four checks above. The Behavioral
  Checklist asks you the same countable questions, and they are the same
  questions to ask of every module you and an AI write together from
  now on.

modelExamples.caption: A pure rename — identical behavior, line for line — moved the class from borrowed vocabulary (Manager, Process, Item, Data, temp) into the clinic's Ubiquitous Language. Before: grep for the domain words finds nothing, and every reader re-derives what ProcessItem means. After: the code and the domain expert's sentence are the same sentence.

The one-sentence test did the design work: "OrderService prices the order and emails the confirmation" needed an "and", so it was two classes wearing one vague name. Named honestly, OrderPricer and ConfirmationMailer each carry a whole sentence, and callers can finally use one job without buying the other.

Scope-honest renaming, behavior untouched: GetSubscriber registered strangers and IsActive wrote history, so both names were lies every caller believed. FindOrRegisterSubscriber and RecordCheckAndReportActive tell the truth — and the second name, needing "And", immediately exposes the next refactor. Honest names turn hidden design flaws into visible, countable ones.

exercises.title: Rename a lending desk into the library's language
exercises.smell: Off-domain and dishonest names: the lending desk behaves correctly and the boundary Test Suite starts green, but nothing behind the Target Interface speaks the library's language. The internals are written in borrowed vocabulary — Manager, Process, Data, item, temp, flag — the same domain concept goes by several names in different corners, and several names lie about scope: a Get that creates, a Check that mutates. Rename everything behind the Target Interface into the library's own terms (the glossary in smell-notes.md), Test Suite green after every rename.

exercises.title: Build a front desk that speaks the hotel's language
exercises.smell: The construct temptation is to let implementation vocabulary write the code: dictionaries named dict, loop variables named item, booleans named flag, a helper named Manager — behavior a Test Suite accepts but no hotelier could read. The folder README carries the hotel glossary — guest, room, stay, check-in, check-out, occupied, vacant — and every class, method, and variable you add draws its words from it, each private member's responsibility fitting one sentence without 'and'.

checklistQuestions.prompt: Grep your solution for Manager, Helper, Util, Handler, Process, Data, Info, temp, flag, item, and obj. Outside the Target Interface file, is the hit count zero?

options.label: No — at least one vague name remains

checklistQuestions.prompt: State each class's and each private method's responsibility in one sentence starting with its name. Did any sentence need 'and'?

options.label: No — every sentence came out whole

checklistQuestions.prompt: For each member you named, read only the name and signature and write down what you expect it to do; then read the body. Count the members that did more, less, or other than the name promised (a Get that creates, an Is that records). Is the count zero?

options.label: Yes — every name kept its promise
